pos: n. (Aegidius Hunnius, 1550–1603, Lutheran theologian at Marburg and Wittenberg)
etymology: Greek Aigidios through Latin Aegidius, of the kid, a shield; Hunnius, latinised from the German surname Hunn.
biblical_def: Aegidius Hunnius taught at Marburg and then at Wittenberg, and was among the most active controversialists of the second Lutheran generation, writing against Rome, against the Reformed and against the antitrinitarians. His best work is on the person of Christ and on the Godhead of the Son, where he argued the eternal deity of the Word from the Old Testament as well as the New with real care, and where the dictionary gladly stands beside him. His worst is the use he made of the same Christology to defend the bodily presence of Christ's human nature in the Supper, by arguing that the properties of the divine nature are communicated to the human so that Christ's body may be everywhere the bread is. The dictionary honours the first and names the second as error. Hunnius is a useful case of how a true doctrine pressed past its warrant produces a false one: the hypostatic union is real, and it does not make the body of Christ ubiquitous.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ubiquity as omnipresence, and hypostatical union as the union of the divine and human natures in Christ.
webster_full: UBIQ'UITY, n. Omnipresence; existence in all places at the same time.
HYPOSTAT'ICAL, a. Constitutive; personal; as the hypostatical union of the two natures in Christ.
COMMUNICA'TION, n. The act of imparting; that which is imparted or bestowed.
POLEM'IC, a. Controversial; disputative; engaged in controversy.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Act 3:21
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
Heb 8:1
Now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens;
Col 3:1
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
corruption_summary: Sound on the Godhead of the Son, and wrong in using that doctrine to make Christ's body present in the bread.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is the Lutheran doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's human nature, built on a particular reading of the communication of attributes within the hypostatic union. Hunnius held that because the Person is one, the divine omnipresence may be communicated to the human nature, so that Christ's body is truly and bodily present wherever the Supper is celebrated. The Reformed answer is not that the union is weak but that the natures remain distinct in the union: the human nature retains what belongs to a human nature, including a location, and Scripture plainly locates it.

The standard is where the New Testament puts the ascended body. “Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things” (Act 3:21). “We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens” (Heb 8:1). The believer is told to look there and not to a table: “seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God” (Col 3:1). And the article Hunnius defended well remains true and is confessed here with him — “and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1).

“Whom the heaven must receive” (Act 3:21) — the answer to a ubiquitous body.
“where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God” (Col 3:1) — the locus the Reformed will not surrender.

pos: n. (Matthias Hafenreffer, 1561–1619, Lutheran theologian at Tubingen and teacher of Kepler)
etymology: Hebrew Mattithyah through Greek Matthias, gift of the LORD; German Hafenreffer, a potter's surname.
biblical_def: Matthias Hafenreffer taught theology at Tubingen, where his Loci Theologici became a standard text in Lutheran Germany and in Sweden, and where Johannes Kepler was among his students and remained his correspondent. The letters between them are worth more than the textbook. Kepler, a Lutheran who could not subscribe the Formula of Concord's doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's body and was barred from the Supper for it, wrote to his old teacher about the heavens and about his exclusion; Hafenreffer answered with real affection and would not move on the doctrine. The dictionary records the exchange because it shows the cost of the ubiquity doctrine inside Lutheranism itself: it fenced the Supper against one of the most devout astronomers in Europe, whose scruple was precisely the Reformed one, that a human body is somewhere. Hafenreffer was kind, learned and wrong on the point, and his pupil paid for it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excommunicate as to expel from the communion of a church, and astronomy as the science of the heavenly bodies.
webster_full: EXCOMMU'NICATE, v.t. To expel from communion; to eject from the communion of the church and deprive of spiritual advantages.
ASTRON'OMY, n. The science which teaches the knowledge of the celestial bodies, their magnitudes, motions and distances.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. The act of subscribing; attestation given by underwriting the name.
FENCE, v.t. To guard; to enclose; to secure, as to fence the table of the Lord.
scriptures: Psa 19:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Act 3:21
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
Rom 14:4
Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
corruption_summary: Kepler's teacher, kind and immovable, whose church barred his pupil from the Supper over Christ's ubiquity.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is again the ubiquity of Christ's human nature, and here its pastoral consequence. Kepler held the gospel, the Creed and the Augsburg Confession, and was excluded from the Lord's table because he would not affirm that Christ's body is bodily present in the bread. A doctrine that is not in Scripture had become a term of communion, and a believing man was fenced out by it.

The standard is the self-examination Scripture actually requires at the table and the limits of our judgment of a brother. “But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup” (1Co 11:28) — the test is of the man's own heart, not of a scholastic formula. “Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth” (Rom 14:4). Meanwhile the heavens Kepler measured keep their own testimony: “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork” (Psa 19:1).

pos: n. (Balthasar Meisner, 1587–1626, Wittenberg theologian, author of the Sober Philosophy)
etymology: Akkadian through Hebrew Belteshazzar, the traditional name of one of the eastern magi; German Meisner, of Meissen.
biblical_def: Balthasar Meisner taught at Wittenberg and died at thirty-nine, leaving among other works the Philosophia Sobria, an examination of how far philosophy may be used in theology and where it must stop. His answer was that reason is a true instrument in its own sphere, serves well in defining terms and detecting fallacies, and has no authority to decide what God has revealed; where philosophy contradicts Scripture, philosophy is wrong. The dictionary commends that answer and commends the title. Sober is exactly the right word, and the two intemperate alternatives were as common then as now: a theology that lets Aristotle set the agenda, and a piety that refuses to think and calls the refusal faith. Meisner, a confessional Lutheran who differed from the Reformed on the Supper and on election, is on this question a reliable guide, and the dictionary says so without pretending the other differences away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sober as temperate and not intoxicated, and philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes and reasons.
webster_full: SO'BER, a. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; not intoxicated; habitually temperate; grave; serious.
PHILOS'OPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of phenomena as explained by and resolved into causes and reasons.
REA'SON, n. A faculty of the mind by which it distinguishes truth from falsehood, and good from evil.
FAL'LACY, n. Deceptive or false appearance; sophism; a deceitful argument.
scriptures: Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: His Sober Philosophy made reason an instrument in theology and denied it any authority over revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the pair of errors Meisner named. One lets a philosophical system set the terms, so that revelation is admitted only where a prevailing account of reality has room for it — the method of every age's accommodating theology, ours included. The other treats all careful thinking as pride and leaves the Christian unable to define a word or follow an argument, which does not protect doctrine but surrenders it to whoever argues most confidently.

The principle to recover is that revelation rules and reason serves. “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19). The apostolic manner of speaking is taught by the Spirit and not by human wisdom: “not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth” (1Co 2:13). And the test is always the same — “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

Greek moria (G3472) — foolishness; 1 Corinthians 3:19.
Greek sugkrino (G4793) — to compare, to join together; 1 Corinthians 2:13.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; Isaiah 8:20.

“the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19) — reason as instrument, not as judge.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — a title that is itself the argument.

pos: n. (Salomon Glassius, 1593–1656, Lutheran theologian of Jena and Gotha, author of the Sacred Philology)
etymology: Hebrew Shelomoh, peaceable; Glassius, latinised from the German surname Glass.
biblical_def: Salomon Glassius was a pupil of Johann Gerhard, professor at Jena and then general superintendent at Gotha, and the author of the Philologia Sacra — a systematic treatment of the grammar, idiom and figures of the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures, and of the rules by which a passage is to be interpreted. It was used for two centuries by Lutherans and Reformed alike, and it is one of the works that made the grammatical-historical reading of Scripture a discipline rather than an instinct. He also oversaw the annotated Weimar Bible. The dictionary commends the book and notes what became of its method. Glassius taught that the sense of Scripture is one and is found by grammar and context under the Spirit's teaching, and that figures are to be recognised rather than invented. The later historical-critical school kept his grammar and dropped his premise that the text is God's own word and therefore true; the tools are the same and the results are opposite.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philology as the study of words and literature, and idiom as a mode of expression peculiar to a language.
webster_full: PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words; that branch of literature which comprehends a knowledge of the etymology of words and their construction.
ID'IOM, n. A mode of expression peculiar to a language; a peculiarity of expression or phraseology.
TROPE, n. A word or expression used in a different sense from that which it properly possesses; a figure.
EXEGE'SIS, n. Exposition; explanation; interpretation.
scriptures: Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture cannot be broken;
corruption_summary: His Sacred Philology made grammatical interpretation a discipline; the critics later kept the grammar and dropped the premise.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the historical-critical method, which inherited the philological apparatus Glassius and his generation built and used it on a different assumption: that the biblical books are human documents whose claims about their own authorship, date and divine origin are to be reconstructed against them. Under that assumption Moses did not write the Pentateuch, Isaiah is a committee, Daniel is late, and the miracles are literary. The tools — grammar, idiom, context, figures — are legitimate and were sharpened by believing men. The premise is what changed.

The standard is Scripture's testimony about itself. “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20); “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21). Our Lord's own premise is unbreakable: “the scripture cannot be broken” (Joh 10:35). And the aim of all honest interpretation is still the aim of the Levites at the water gate — they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).

pos: n. (Johann Conrad Dannhauer, 1603–1666, Strasbourg theologian and teacher of Spener)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Germanic Konrad, bold counsel; Dannhauer, dweller by the fir wood.
biblical_def: Johann Conrad Dannhauer was professor and chief preacher at Strasbourg for some forty years, and the author of the Idea Boni Interpretis, a treatise on what a good interpreter is and does, which treated interpretation as a general art before applying it to Scripture. He also preached an enormous catechetical course on the Ten Commandments. Among his students was Philipp Jakob Spener, whose later Pia Desideria launched German Pietism; Spener always acknowledged what he owed to Dannhauer's preaching and to his insistence that doctrine must reach the conscience and the household. The dictionary records that line of descent with the discrimination it requires. Dannhauer's demand that orthodoxy be preached into living men was right, and the dictionary says so; what Pietism afterward made of it, when the demand for inward experience began to loosen the hold of confession and doctrine, is a different matter and is treated under its own head.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines interpreter as one who explains or expounds, and hermeneutics as the art of interpretation.
webster_full: INTERP'RETER, n. One that explains or expounds; an expositor.
HERMENEU'TICS, n. The art or science of interpretation, particularly of the Scriptures.
CAT'ECHETICAL, a. Relating to oral instruction, particularly in the first principles of the Christian religion.
CON'SCIENCE, n. The faculty or principle which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our actions.
scriptures: Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
Jam 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
corruption_summary: Spener's teacher, who demanded that orthodoxy be preached into consciences and households.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse lies on both sides of Dannhauer. Behind him stands a confessional preaching that could become the recitation of correct propositions to people whose lives were untouched; after him comes a movement that answered the deadness by elevating inward experience until the confession itself grew optional. He himself held the right thing: that the doctrine is true, that it must be opened so plainly that a servant understands it, and that it must be obeyed.

The principle to recover is that teaching aims at understanding and ends in practice. The Levites “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Philip's question to the eunuch assumes that a hearer may be reading and not understanding: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). The minister is to watch both halves — “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them” (1Ti 4:16) — and the hearer is warned against the half-way house: “be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only” (Jam 1:22).

Greek anaginosko (G314) — to read, to read aloud; Acts 8:30.
Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, to understand; Nehemiah 8:8.

“Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30) — a treatise on what a good interpreter is.
“be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only” (Jam 1:22) — Spener's acknowledged debt.

pos: n. (Abraham Calov, 1612–1686, Wittenberg theologian, systematician and opponent of syncretism)
etymology: Hebrew Abraham, father of a multitude; Calov, latinised from the German surname Kalau.
biblical_def: Abraham Calov taught at Wittenberg for forty years and produced a systematic theology in twelve volumes, a vast annotated Bible written largely against the readings of Hugo Grotius, and a long shelf of polemic. His principal controversy was with Georg Calixtus of Helmstedt, who proposed that Lutherans, Reformed and Romanists might unite on the Apostles' Creed and the consensus of the first five centuries; Calov opposed that programme as a dissolution of the faith and gave it the name by which it is still known, syncretism. The dictionary judges the controversy in halves. Calov was right that a union built on the first five centuries would quietly surrender justification by faith alone, which is not in the Creed and is in Paul; he was wrong, and sometimes unlovely, in treating the Reformed as the Creed's enemies rather than as brethren who confessed the same gospel and differed on the Supper. His Bible, as it happens, was the copy Johann Sebastian Bach owned and annotated.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines syncretism as the attempted union of different systems, and systematic as formed with regular connection of parts.
webster_full: SYN'CRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance with each other.
SYSTEMAT'IC, a. Methodical; formed with regular connection and adaptation of parts to each other.
CONSENT', n. Agreement of minds in opinion; accord.
POLEM'ICS, n. Controversy; the practice of disputation on points of doctrine.
scriptures: Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
corruption_summary: He named and fought syncretism, rightly on justification and wrongly in treating the Reformed as enemies.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is syncretism as Calov defined it: a union of churches purchased by reducing the faith to what all parties can still say, which in practice means the ancient creeds without the article the Reformation recovered. The Apostles' Creed does not teach justification by faith alone; a communion built on the Creed alone can therefore include Trent. Calov saw that and was right. The corresponding modern form is any ecumenism that treats the gospel's instrumental cause as a secondary matter.

The standard is Paul's refusal at Jerusalem and his conclusion in Romans. “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5). “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). The faith was delivered once and is to be contended for: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). And the aim of all of it is a church that is not blown about — “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14) — which is a different thing from a church at war with its brethren.

pos: n. (Johann Andreas Quenstedt, 1617–1688, Wittenberg theologian, author of the Didactic-Polemical Theology)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; German Quenstedt, a place-name surname of Saxony.
biblical_def: Johann Andreas Quenstedt taught at Wittenberg for forty years and left the Theologia Didactico-Polemica, the most complete statement of seventeenth-century Lutheran orthodoxy: each doctrine stated, defined, proved from Scripture, then defended against every opponent in order, with the objections set out fairly and answered one by one. He has been called the bookkeeper of Lutheran orthodoxy, and the name is fair in both directions. The dictionary admires the method and uses the book. A theology written that way can be checked: the reader sees the proof texts, the opponent's best case and the answer, and can judge for himself. The Reformed reader will judge against Quenstedt on the Supper, on the extent of the atonement and on the possibility of falling from grace, and will find that Quenstedt has stated the Reformed case accurately before disagreeing with it — which is a courtesy not every polemicist of that century managed, and worth imitating.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines didactic as fitted or intended to teach, and polemical as controversial, disputative.
webster_full: DIDAC'TIC, a. Fitted or intended to teach; preceptive; containing doctrines or precepts.
POLEM'ICAL, a. Controversial; disputative; engaged in supporting an opinion by argument.
OBJEC'TION, n. That which is or may be offered against an opinion or measure.
THESIS, n. A position or proposition which a person advances and offers to maintain.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: His great dogmatics states each opponent's best case before answering it, including the Reformed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the polemical habit of answering a caricature. It is quicker, it satisfies one's own side, and it persuades nobody who holds the position attacked. Quenstedt's practice was to state the opposing view as its best advocates stated it, with citations, and then to answer. That practice costs time and it is the only kind of polemic that is honest.

The principle to recover is that an answer must follow a hearing. “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13). The Christian is to be ready with a reason and to give it in the right spirit: “with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). The elder must be able “to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9), which presupposes knowing what they actually say. And the Berean standard applies to the defender as much as to the hearer — “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).

Greek prautes (G4240) — meekness, gentleness of spirit; 1 Peter 3:15.
Greek antilego (G483) — to speak against, to gainsay; Titus 1:9.
Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, to listen; Proverbs 18:13.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift; Acts 17:11.

“with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15) — a courtesy not every polemicist of that century managed.

pos: n. (Johann Benedict Carpzov, 1607–1657, Leipzig theologian and expositor of the Lutheran symbols)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Latin Benedictus, blessed; Carpzov, a Saxon surname.
biblical_def: Johann Benedict Carpzov belonged to a Leipzig dynasty of lawyers and theologians and taught at Leipzig as professor and superintendent. His useful book is an introduction to the symbolical books of the Lutheran churches — the Augsburg Confession, the Apology, the Catechisms, the Formula of Concord — setting out when each was written, against what, and in what sense each article is to be taken. He also wrote a guide to theological study. The dictionary values the genre. A confession that is subscribed without being understood becomes either a dead form or a party badge, and the remedy is exactly what Carpzov supplied: a plain account of the historical occasion and the intended sense of each article, so that a man who subscribes knows what he is saying. The Reformed churches have the same need and have produced the same kind of book, and this entry commends the discipline rather than the Lutheran content of these particular symbols.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines symbolical books as the formularies of faith of a church, and isagogic as introductory.
webster_full: SYMBOL'ICAL, a. Representing by signs; as the symbolical books of a church, containing its formularies of faith.
ISAGOG'IC, a. Introductory; relating to an introduction to a science or a body of writings.
SUBSCRIP'TION, n. Attestation given by underwriting the name; assent to a formulary.
SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of some place, person or business.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them. And all the people shall say, Amen.
corruption_summary: He wrote the plain account of what each Lutheran symbol says and why, so that subscription could be honest.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is subscription without comprehension, in two forms. In the first, a minister signs a confession he has not read and holds whatever he likes; in the second, a confession becomes a tribal marker whose content nobody consults and whose words are used as slogans. Both are cured by knowing what the document was written to say.

The principle to recover is that a profession is a statement with content, made before witnesses, and binding. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13). Timothy's own case is cited as the pattern: he “hast professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1Ti 6:12). The profession is to be held without wavering — “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23) — and in the covenant at Shechem the people said Amen to words they had heard read: “Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them. And all the people shall say, Amen” (Deu 27:26).

pos: n. (Johann Olearius, 1611–1684, Lutheran court preacher at Halle and Weissenfels, hymnwriter)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Latin Olearius, of oil, latinised from the German surname Oelschlegel.
biblical_def: Johann Olearius was court preacher and general superintendent in the Saxon duchy of Weissenfels, a prolific devotional author, the compiler of one of the largest German hymnbooks of the century, and the writer of hymns still sung in English, among them the Advent hymn on the fortieth of Isaiah that begins with the prophet's own doubled command to comfort. He also produced a commentary on the whole Bible. The dictionary names him because of what a hymn does. The Lutheran dogmaticians in this batch wrote in Latin for men who had been to university; Olearius put the same gospel into German verse for people who could not read Latin and would never own a folio, and his lines were carried in memory into fields, sickrooms and graves. A church needs both labours and usually honours only the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comfort as to strengthen and console, and hymn as a song or ode in honour of God.
webster_full: COM'FORT, v.t. To strengthen; to invigorate; to cheer or enliven; to console in affliction.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God; a sacred song.
AD'VENT, n. A coming; appropriately, the coming of our Saviour.
DEVO'TIONAL, a. Pertaining to devotion; used in devotion.
scriptures: Isa 40:1
Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.
Isa 40:2
Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD'S hand double for all her sins.
Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: A court preacher who put the gospel of the dogmaticians into German verse that ordinary people carried by heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of hymnody as the emotional annex of a service, written to a mood and replaced when the mood changes. Olearius wrote hymns that teach: his Advent hymn is an exposition of a chapter of Isaiah, with the doctrine of pardon, the forerunner and the coming of the Lord all in it, in a form a child could memorise.

The principle to recover is that song is a means of teaching and that God Himself gives the words of comfort. “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God” (Isa 40:1) — the command is doubled and it is His. The content follows: “that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned” (Isa 40:2). The soul is charged to remember: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2). And singing is explicitly a form of teaching — “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16).

pos: n. (David Hollaz, 1648–1713, the last of the great Lutheran dogmaticians)
biblical_def: David Hollaz was a Pomeranian pastor and schoolmaster who in 1707 published the Examen Theologicum Acroamaticum, the last great system of Lutheran orthodoxy and the one most often reprinted. It is cast in question and answer, follows the order of the older dogmaticians, and differs from them in tone: the ordo salutis is worked out with an attention to the awakening of the sinner and the application of grace that shows the Pietist air he breathed. Within a generation the German faculties had gone over to rationalism and nothing like his book was written again. The dictionary places him here as a closing marker. A tradition's last systematic theologian is worth noticing, because what comes after him is not a better system but the abandonment of the project; and the particular combination in Hollaz — strict orthodox content with a warm concern for the conscience — is the combination every confessional church has to keep, since losing either one has historically cost the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines examen as examination, and rationalism as the practice of regarding reason as the supreme authority in religion.
webster_full: EXA'MEN, n. Examination; disquisition; inquiry.
RA'TIONALISM, n. The system of those who make reason the sole criterion of religious truth.
AWA'KEN, v.t. To rouse from sleep or from a state of spiritual insensibility.
SYS'TEM, n. An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a body of doctrine.
scriptures: Eph 5:14
Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
And brought them out, and said, Sirs, what must I do to be saved?
And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
corruption_summary: The last great Lutheran system, orthodox in content and warm toward the conscience, written as rationalism took the faculties.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the rationalism that replaced this whole enterprise in the German universities within a generation of Hollaz's book: the principle that reason judges revelation, so that whatever in Scripture reason cannot accommodate must be explained away as accommodation, myth or moral allegory. It did not arrive by argument so much as by fashion, and it emptied faculty after faculty. The lesson the dictionary draws is that orthodoxy is never inherited; each generation holds it or loses it.

The standard is a gospel addressed to a conscience and a warning about the appetite that destroyed those faculties. “Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light” (Eph 5:14). The jailer's question and its answer are the whole of what a system exists to serve: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Act 16:30) — “Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved” (Act 16:31). And the mechanism of decline is named in advance: “the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers” (2Ti 4:3).
